Dear Secretary Reese:

        On October 29, 2026, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) submitted, pursuant
to Federal Power Act section 205, 16 U.S.C. § 824d, revisions to the PJM Open Access
Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) to update the Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”)
rules to address, inter alia, issues identified in the Commission’s September 29 Order1
(“October 29 Filing”).2 In the October 29 Filing, PJM requested that proposed new
Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.3A become effective January 29, 2027, and the
remainder of the proposed Tariff revisions become effective February 28, 2027.3 PJM
also sought a one-time, prospective waiver of certain requirements under Tariff,
Attachment DD, section 16.4

        After submitting this filing, PJM discovered that when it entered the metadata for
proposed new Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.3A, PJM incorrectly entered an
effective date of January 15, 2027, instead of January 29, 2027. Accordingly, to correct
this clerical error, PJM submits a corrected version of the sole affected tariff record, i.e.,
proposed new Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.3A only to make the ministerial
revision to the metadata, to be effective January 29, 2027, as proposed in the October 29

Dear Secretary Reese:

           Pursuant to section 205 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”), 1 the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”) Regulations, 2 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.

(“PJM”) hereby submits proposed revisions to the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff

(“Tariff”) that updates the Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”) rules to address,

inter alia, issues identified in the Commission’s September 29 Order. 3 Specifically, this

filing proposes modifications to establish just and reasonable rules to (i) allocate

responsibility for RBP Charges to certain Load Serving Entities (“LSE”); (ii) require LSEs

responsible for RBP Charges to post an appropriate level of credit; and (iii) provide notice

           PJM requests that most of the proposed revisions become effective on February 28,

2027—the same effective date for the RBP rules the Commission accepted in the

September 29 Order. 5 However, because PJM is proposing certain pre-conduct of RBP

Commission issue an order on all aspects of this filing no later than January 29, 2027, to

facilitate conduct of the RBP and provide participants the advance notice necessary for the

efficient administration of the RBP.

           To afford stakeholders adequate time to evaluate the proposed RBP rules changes,

PJM moves for the Commission to establish an extended, 32-day comment period, such

that comments and interventions would be due November 30, 2026. Even accounting for

the intervening holidays and the requested extended comment period, issuance of an order

by January 29, 2027, would still leave the Commission with approximately 60 days

following the close of the comment period to consider the record and act on the filing.

However, the Commission should not feel constrained to wait until January 29, 2027, to

issue an order on the proposed RBP rules, but should feel free to issue an order whenever

it feels appropriate before January 29, 2027.

           In addition, through this filing, PJM also conditionally requests waiver of the

requirement in Tariff, Attachment DD, section 16.2 for PJM to “investigate the cause for

the shortage, and recommend corrective action” 6 in the event the 2029/2030 Base Residual

Auction clears short of the reliability requirement. Likewise, should the 2029/2030

Delivery Year Base Residual Auction clear short, resulting in three consecutive Delivery

Years with insufficient capacity procurement, PJM conditionally requests waiver of the

requirement in Tariff, Attachment DD, section 16.3 that PJM “declare a capacity shortage

and make a filing with FERC for approval to conduct a Reliability Backstop Auction”

following three consecutive Delivery Years in which the Base Residual Auction clears

short. As discussed below in Part IV, the Commission should grant this one-time,

prospective waiver.

I.         BACKGROUND

           On July 31, 2026, PJM filed a comprehensive proposal to establish the RBP, a

targeted, one-time procurement mechanism designed to address emerging resource

adequacy challenges driven principally by the rapid growth of Large Loads and the

resulting acceleration of capacity needs across the PJM Region. 7 In its September 29

Order, the Commission accepted PJM’s proposed RBP framework, but suspended the

Tariff revisions for a period of five months and established additional procedures to further

examine three discrete aspects of the proposal: cost allocation, Transmission Owner exit

provisions, and LSE collateral requirements. 8 While the Commission initiated a paper

hearing and a related proceeding under section 206 of the FPA to develop a more complete

record regarding those issues, it also expressly and strongly encouraged PJM to submit, an

alternative proposal pursuant to its FPA section 205 filing rights to address the concerns

identified in the order. 9

           PJM submits this section 205 filing in accordance with the Commission’s guidance

from the September 29 Order. The revisions proposed herein are carefully tailored to

address the specific issues identified by the Commission while preserving the fundamental

structure and policy objectives of the RBP framework that the Commission otherwise

accepted in the September 29 Order. Consistent with the Commission’s direction, this

filing presents targeted modifications to the RBP’s cost allocation, exit responsibilities, and

collateral provisions that are intended to resolve the Commission’s remaining areas of

concern, strengthen the overall design of the RBP, and facilitate timely implementation of

a mechanism that is needed to address pressing reliability and resource adequacy risks. By

narrowing the issues in dispute and building upon the framework that the Commission has

already found generally just and reasonable, this filing will promote administrative

efficiency, reduce regulatory uncertainty, and enable PJM to move forward with the RBP

on an expedited basis. 10 Through this section 205 filing, PJM has addressed the issues set

for paper hearing in the September 29 Order.

           PJM respectfully submits that each aspect of the filing is just and reasonable.

Nevertheless, to facilitate prompt Commission action and avoid further delay in the

II.        PROPOSED UPDATES THAT ADDRESS ISSUES IDENTIFIED IN THE
           COMMISSION’S SEPTEMBER 29 ORDER

           A.      PJM Proposes Updates that Directly Address the Commission’s RBP Cost
                   Allocation Concerns.

           Under FPA section 205, cost allocation must be grounded in the principle that costs

are assigned to those who cause them or benefit from the facilities and services provided. 12

At the same time, courts have long recognized that cost causation is not a standard of

mathematical precision. Indeed, courts have long recognized that “it would no doubt be

impossible, even if desirable, to formulate a rate scheme with such precision that each

customer—or even customer group—is made to bear the exact cost of the service he

received.” 13 Therefore, costs need not be “allocate[d] . . . with exacting precision.”14

Rather, they need only “be allocated in a manner that is roughly commensurate with the

discretion to evaluate whether a proposed cost allocation reasonably aligns cost

            As an initial matter, the Commission largely agreed with the foundational premise

of PJM’s proposed RBP cost allocation methodology: the costs of procuring new capacity

to address reliability concerns arising from large load growth should be assigned to the

zone/areas experiencing that growth. Specifically, the Commission’s September 29 Order

explained that:

                     allocating RBP costs to Electric Distributor zone/areas based on a
                     “snapshot” of load growth between 2026/2027 and 2028/2029,
                     adjusted down by qualifying offset capacity, may be just and
                     reasonable, because it reasonably assigns costs to those responsible
                     for the near-term capacity shortfall. Thus, such zone/areas benefit
                     from procurement of new resources to fill this urgent gap. We
                     generally find that PJM’s proposal to initially assign RBP costs to
                     Electric Distributor zone/areas, with the ultimate cost allocation to
                     the LSEs as determined by the state and/or [Relevant Electric Retail
                     Regulatory Authority (“RERRA”)] and as reported to the Electric
                     Distributor by PJM, may be just and reasonable, as it reflects the
                     authority of PJM under the Tariff and respects the authority of the
                     states and/or RERRAs. 17

            The Commission’s concerns were therefore not directed at the underlying cost

allocation to the zone/area. Rather, the Commission questioned whether PJM’s use of Load

Adjustment data provided the most accurate means of identifying the Large Load growth

with “relying on Load Adjustments to measure load growth [because that] may be

inconsistent or not reasonably capture forecasted load growth or actual large load

growth.” 19 That is, some large loads may be reflected in PJM’s underlying load forecast

rather than in the incremental Load Adjustments used in PJM’s initial proposal.20

Consequently, the Commission was concerned that the use of the Load Adjustment delta

“could lead to the costs imposed on certain entities not being at least roughly commensurate

with the benefits they will receive from the procurement.” 21

           This filing directly addresses the Commission’s concern by allocating the “RBP

costs to the Electric Distributor zone/areas with the reported new load that is driving the

need for the procurement.” 22 Specifically, rather than relying on Load Adjustment data as

a proxy for Large Load growth, PJM is proposing to require Electric Distributors outside

of a Fixed Resource Requirement (“FRR”) Service Area to report, by no later than seven

days prior to the commencement of the RBP, the aggregate incremental peak Large Load

growth between the 2026 actual summer peak and the 2028/2029 Delivery Year expected

summer peak to PJM. 23 This updated approach will better align cost responsibility with

                   1.       Requiring Electric Distributors to report the Large Load increase
                            between 2026 and the expected 2028/2029 Delivery Year will allow
                            RBP cost allocation to all incremental Large Loads.

           Requiring each Electric Distributor to report the aggregate incremental Large Load

growth between the 2026 actual summer peak and the 2028/2029 Delivery Year expected

summer peak is consistent with Commission precedent. 24 Indeed, Electric Distributors

already report actual and forecasted peak loads to PJM today. This proposal merely

requires Electric Distributors to provide a more granular subset of information relating

specifically to Large Load growth. Under this proposal, each Electric Distributor outside

an FRR Service Area will be required to report the aggregate incremental quantity of Large

Load, where the Large Load quantity for each load is calculated as the difference between:

(1) the actual summer peak load associated with the Large Load in 2026; and (2) the

expected summer peak load associated with Large Load for the 2028/2029 Delivery Year. 25

Additionally, Electric Distributors will be required to report the identity of the Large Load

that is supported by an electric service obligation, construction commitment, or equivalent

agreement. 26 Because Electric Distributors maintain the direct distribution and metering

relationships associated with these loads and already serve as PJM’s primary source of

           Consistent with PJM’s load forecasting process, the expected quantity of Large

Load for the 2028/2029 Delivery Year reported under this proposal should largely align

with the information the Electric Distributor previously provided to PJM for development

of the applicable load forecast. However, because Large Load development is dynamic,

circumstances may change after submission of forecast data and before the reporting of

Large Load values for purposes of establishing the Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”)

procurement targets. This could potentially include new Large Loads that are now

expected to be online by the 2028/2029 Delivery Year that may not have previously been

expected at the time PJM developed the load forecast. Conversely, there could be electric

service agreements with Large Loads that are canceled between the time Electric

Distributors initially reported the data as part of PJM’s load forecast process and when the

Electric Distributors report expected Large Loads for RBP purposes. In either case, the

proposal requires an Electric Distributor to “provide an explanation for any deviation

between the expected quantity of Large Loads for the 2028/2029 Delivery Year and the

values provided by the Electric Distributor to [PJM] as part of the development for the load

forecast.” 27 As always, PJM maintains the ability to refer Electric Distributors to the

Commission’s Office of Enforcement in the event the reported information is significantly

different from what the Electric Distributor reported as part of PJM’s load forecast

development process and such deviations are not sufficiently explained. This requirement

safeguards against potential incorrect submissions while allowing PJM to rely on the most

           The proposed approach also satisfies the Commission’s cost-causation standards

because it assigns costs in a manner that is roughly commensurate with the benefits

received. 28 Cost causation requires that “all approved rates reflect to some degree the costs

actually caused by the customer who must pay them.” 29 Indeed, as the courts have held,

“nothing requires the Commission to ensure full or perfect cost causation,” 30 and the

Commission “is not bound to reject any rate mechanism that tracks the cost causation

principle less than perfectly.” 31

           Here, the data reported by Electric Distributors represent the most practical and

administratively feasible measure of incremental Large Load growth for purposes of

establishing a cost allocation approach that will assign costs to the zone/areas where the

incremental Large Loads will be located. While no cost allocation methodology can

achieve perfect precision, the Commission has repeatedly recognized that feasibility

considerations are relevant and that cost-causation principles need only be applied in a

reasonably accurate and practical manner. 32 By relying on Electric Distributor’s reported

           To be clear, the information required under this proposal will initially be reported

separately from the Large Load Registry that the Commission recently accepted because

the information required from the Electric Distributors serves a different purpose.

Specifically, the reporting requirement here is targeted to quantify incremental Large Load

growth between 2026 and the 2028/2029 Delivery Year for purposes of establishing the

Initial RBP Target. Nonetheless, to the extent appropriate, certain information submitted

through this process may ultimately be incorporated into the Large Load Registry.

                    2.      RBP costs will be allocated to the zone/areas associated with
                            incremental Large Loads.

           Based on information provided by Electric Distributors, PJM will allocate the

Initial RBP Target among Electric Distributor zone/areas in proportion to each zone/area’s

share of the total incremental Large Load growth. PJM will then reduce a zone/area’s

allocated share to the extent PJM receives the requisite evidence, as detailed in Tariff,

Attachment DD, section 18.2(c), 33 of new capacity in the form of Qualifying RBP Offset

UCAP MW that is the subject of a bilateral agreement with a Large Load. 34 In addition,

to the extent an Electric Distributor requests, with the required accompanying support

           This approach is consistent with the Commission’s determination that “[a]llocating

RBP costs based on a snapshot of this shortfall over the term of the RBP commitment

period may provide greater certainty to the LSEs in the Electric Distributor zone/areas

ultimately bearing responsibility for those costs.” 37           Accordingly, PJM proposes to

continue using a snapshot of incremental Large Load growth between the 2026 summer

peak and the forecasted summer peak for the 2028/2029 Delivery Year to establish each

zone/area’s share of the Final RBP Target MW. That allocation to the zone/area will

remain fixed throughout the 15-year RBP commitment period. Maintaining a fixed

allocation to the zone/area promotes certainty, provides transparent cost responsibility at

the outset of the commitment period, and avoids repeated reallocation of costs to different

zone/areas during the term of the RBP Resource commitment.

granularly allocated to LSEs within an Electric Distributor’s zone/area. As noted, above,

the September 29 Order held that “the ultimate cost allocation to the LSEs as determined

by the state and/or RERRA and as reported to the Electric Distributor . . . may be just and

reasonable[.]” 38 Specifically, RBP Charges may be allocated based on “the state and/or

Dear Secretary Reese:

           Pursuant to section 205 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”),1 the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”) Regulations,2 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.

(“PJM”) hereby submits proposed revisions to the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff

(“Tariff”) that updates the Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”) rules to address,

inter alia, issues identified in the Commission’s September 29 Order.3 Specifically, this

filing proposes modifications to establish just and reasonable rules to (i) allocate

responsibility for RBP Charges to certain Load Serving Entities (“LSE”); (ii) require LSEs

responsible for RBP Charges to post an appropriate level of credit; and (iii) provide notice

to LSEs exiting PJM of their continuing responsibility for RBP Charges allocated to them

through the remainder of the RBP commitment term.4

           PJM requests that most of the proposed revisions become effective on February 28,

facilitate conduct of the RBP and provide participants the advance notice necessary for the

efficient administration of the RBP.

           To afford stakeholders adequate time to evaluate the proposed RBP rules changes,

PJM moves for the Commission to establish an extended, 32-day comment period, such

that comments and interventions would be due November 30, 2026. Even accounting for

the intervening holidays and the requested extended comment period, issuance of an order

by January 29, 2027, would still leave the Commission with approximately 60 days

following the close of the comment period to consider the record and act on the filing.

However, the Commission should not feel constrained to wait until January 29, 2027, to

issue an order on the proposed RBP rules, but should feel free to issue an order whenever

it feels appropriate before January 29, 2027.

           In addition, through this filing, PJM also conditionally requests waiver of the

requirement in Tariff, Attachment DD, section 16.2 for PJM to “investigate the cause for

the shortage, and recommend corrective action”6 in the event the 2029/2030 Base Residual

Auction clears short of the reliability requirement. Likewise, should the 2029/2030

Delivery Year Base Residual Auction clear short, resulting in three consecutive Delivery

Years with insufficient capacity procurement, PJM conditionally requests waiver of the

requirement in Tariff, Attachment DD, section 16.3 that PJM “declare a capacity shortage

and make a filing with FERC for approval to conduct a Reliability Backstop Auction”

following three consecutive Delivery Years in which the Base Residual Auction clears

short. As discussed below in Part IV, the Commission should grant this one-time,

prospective waiver.

I.         BACKGROUND

           On July 31, 2026, PJM filed a comprehensive proposal to establish the RBP, a

targeted, one-time procurement mechanism designed to address emerging resource

adequacy challenges driven principally by the rapid growth of Large Loads and the

resulting acceleration of capacity needs across the PJM Region.7 In its September 29

Order, the Commission accepted PJM’s proposed RBP framework, but suspended the

Tariff revisions for a period of five months and established additional procedures to further

examine three discrete aspects of the proposal: cost allocation, Transmission Owner exit

provisions, and LSE collateral requirements.8 While the Commission initiated a paper

hearing and a related proceeding under section 206 of the FPA to develop a more complete

record regarding those issues, it also expressly and strongly encouraged PJM to submit, an

alternative proposal pursuant to its FPA section 205 filing rights to address the concerns

identified in the order.9

           PJM submits this section 205 filing in accordance with the Commission’s guidance

from the September 29 Order. The revisions proposed herein are carefully tailored to

address the specific issues identified by the Commission while preserving the fundamental

structure and policy objectives of the RBP framework that the Commission otherwise

accepted in the September 29 Order. Consistent with the Commission’s direction, this

filing presents targeted modifications to the RBP’s cost allocation, exit responsibilities, and

collateral provisions that are intended to resolve the Commission’s remaining areas of

concern, strengthen the overall design of the RBP, and facilitate timely implementation of

a mechanism that is needed to address pressing reliability and resource adequacy risks. By

narrowing the issues in dispute and building upon the framework that the Commission has

already found generally just and reasonable, this filing will promote administrative

efficiency, reduce regulatory uncertainty, and enable PJM to move forward with the RBP

on an expedited basis.10 Through this section 205 filing, PJM has addressed the issues set

for paper hearing in the September 29 Order.

           PJM respectfully submits that each aspect of the filing is just and reasonable.

Nevertheless, to facilitate prompt Commission action and avoid further delay in the

to the extent permitted under section 205 of the FPA and NRG Power Marketing, LLC v.

accepting the remainder of the filing. Such an approach, if deemed necessary by the

Commission, would preserve the benefits of the proposed reforms and support the timely

II.        PROPOSED UPDATES THAT ADDRESS ISSUES IDENTIFIED IN THE
           COMMISSION’S SEPTEMBER 29 ORDER

           A.      PJM Proposes Updates that Directly Address the Commission’s RBP Cost
                   Allocation Concerns.

           Under FPA section 205, cost allocation must be grounded in the principle that costs

are assigned to those who cause them or benefit from the facilities and services provided.12

At the same time, courts have long recognized that cost causation is not a standard of

mathematical precision. Indeed, courts have long recognized that “it would no doubt be

impossible, even if desirable, to formulate a rate scheme with such precision that each

customer—or even customer group—is made to bear the exact cost of the service he

received.”13 Therefore, costs need not be “allocate[d] . . . with exacting precision.”14

Rather, they need only “be allocated in a manner that is roughly commensurate with the



11

12
   E.g., Pub. Serv. Elec. & Gas Co. v. FERC, 989 F.3d 10, 13 (D.C. Cir. 2021) (The Commission “has long
viewed the just-and-reasonable requirement” under FPA section 205 “to incorporate a cost-causation
principle.” (internal quotation marks and citation omitted)); Ill. Com. Comm’n v. FERC, 576 F.3d 470, 476
(7th Cir. 2009).
13

L.P. v. FERC, 285 F.3d 1, 5 (D.C. Cir. 2002) (explaining the Court has consistently upheld rates based on
cost-causation principles as applied in Alabama Electric Cooperative).
14

1369 (D.C. Cir. 2004)).

benefits received.”15 Consistent with this standard, the Commission possesses broad

discretion to evaluate whether a proposed cost allocation reasonably aligns cost

responsibility with causation and benefits.16

            As an initial matter, the Commission largely agreed with the foundational premise

of PJM’s proposed RBP cost allocation methodology: the costs of procuring new capacity

to address reliability concerns arising from large load growth should be assigned to the

zone/areas experiencing that growth. Specifically, the Commission’s September 29 Order

explained that:

                     allocating RBP costs to Electric Distributor zone/areas based on a
                     “snapshot” of load growth between 2026/2027 and 2028/2029,
                     adjusted down by qualifying offset capacity, may be just and
                     reasonable, because it reasonably assigns costs to those responsible
                     for the near-term capacity shortfall. Thus, such zone/areas benefit
                     from procurement of new resources to fill this urgent gap. We
                     generally find that PJM’s proposal to initially assign RBP costs to
                     Electric Distributor zone/areas, with the ultimate cost allocation to
                     the LSEs as determined by the state and/or [Relevant Electric Retail
                     Regulatory Authority (“RERRA”)] and as reported to the Electric
                     Distributor by PJM, may be just and reasonable, as it reflects the
                     authority of PJM under the Tariff and respects the authority of the
                     states and/or RERRAs.17

            The Commission’s concerns were therefore not directed at the underlying cost

allocation to the zone/area. Rather, the Commission questioned whether PJM’s use of Load

Adjustment data provided the most accurate means of identifying the Large Load growth

alteration omitted).
16

that is driving the need for the RBP.18 More particularly, the Commission was concerned

with “relying on Load Adjustments to measure load growth [because that] may be

inconsistent or not reasonably capture forecasted load growth or actual large load

growth.”19 That is, some large loads may be reflected in PJM’s underlying load forecast

rather than in the incremental Load Adjustments used in PJM’s initial proposal.20

Consequently, the Commission was concerned that the use of the Load Adjustment delta

“could lead to the costs imposed on certain entities not being at least roughly commensurate

with the benefits they will receive from the procurement.”21

           This filing directly addresses the Commission’s concern by allocating the “RBP

costs to the Electric Distributor zone/areas with the reported new load that is driving the

need for the procurement.”22 Specifically, rather than relying on Load Adjustment data as

a proxy for Large Load growth, PJM is proposing to require Electric Distributors outside

of a Fixed Resource Requirement (“FRR”) Service Area to report, by no later than seven

days prior to the commencement of the RBP, the aggregate incremental peak Large Load

growth between the 2026 actual summer peak and the 2028/2029 Delivery Year expected

summer peak to PJM.23 This updated approach will better align cost responsibility with

the specific Large Load growth that necessitates the RBP while preserving the cost-

allocation framework that the Commission otherwise found to be just and reasonable.

                   1.       Requiring Electric Distributors to report the Large Load increase
                            between 2026 and the expected 2028/2029 Delivery Year will allow
                            RBP cost allocation to all incremental Large Loads.

           Requiring each Electric Distributor to report the aggregate incremental Large Load

growth between the 2026 actual summer peak and the 2028/2029 Delivery Year expected

summer peak is consistent with Commission precedent.24 Indeed, Electric Distributors

already report actual and forecasted peak loads to PJM today. This proposal merely

requires Electric Distributors to provide a more granular subset of information relating

specifically to Large Load growth. Under this proposal, each Electric Distributor outside

an FRR Service Area will be required to report the aggregate incremental quantity of Large

Load, where the Large Load quantity for each load is calculated as the difference between:

(1) the actual summer peak load associated with the Large Load in 2026; and (2) the

expected summer peak load associated with Large Load for the 2028/2029 Delivery Year.25

Additionally, Electric Distributors will be required to report the identity of the Large Load

that is supported by an electric service obligation, construction commitment, or equivalent

agreement.26 Because Electric Distributors maintain the direct distribution and metering

relationships associated with these loads and already serve as PJM’s primary source of

L.L.C., 188 FERC ¶ 61,200, at P 40 & n.65 (2024) (finding that an “Electric Distributor is the party with the
distribution and metering facilities defining a zone/area and responsible for reporting load information to
PJM,” and also noting that, “under the current framework, each LSE already reports their peak load
contribution to the Electric Distributor, which is the entity ultimately responsible for reporting that
information to PJM”).

zonal load information, they are uniquely and aptly positioned to provide the most accurate

and comprehensive information regarding incremental Large Load growth.

           Consistent with PJM’s load forecasting process, the expected quantity of Large

Load for the 2028/2029 Delivery Year reported under this proposal should largely align

with the information the Electric Distributor previously provided to PJM for development

of the applicable load forecast. However, because Large Load development is dynamic,

circumstances may change after submission of forecast data and before the reporting of

Large Load values for purposes of establishing the Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”)

procurement targets. This could potentially include new Large Loads that are now

expected to be online by the 2028/2029 Delivery Year that may not have previously been

expected at the time PJM developed the load forecast. Conversely, there could be electric

service agreements with Large Loads that are canceled between the time Electric

Distributors initially reported the data as part of PJM’s load forecast process and when the

Electric Distributors report expected Large Loads for RBP purposes. In either case, the

proposal requires an Electric Distributor to “provide an explanation for any deviation

between the expected quantity of Large Loads for the 2028/2029 Delivery Year and the

values provided by the Electric Distributor to [PJM] as part of the development for the load

forecast.”27 As always, PJM maintains the ability to refer Electric Distributors to the

Commission’s Office of Enforcement in the event the reported information is significantly

different from what the Electric Distributor reported as part of PJM’s load forecast

development process and such deviations are not sufficiently explained. This requirement




27
     Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.3A.
 Debbie-Anne Reese, Secretary
October 29, 2026
Page 10

safeguards against potential incorrect submissions while allowing PJM to rely on the most

current available information.

           The proposed approach also satisfies the Commission’s cost-causation standards

because it assigns costs in a manner that is roughly commensurate with the benefits

received.28 Cost causation requires that “all approved rates reflect to some degree the costs

actually caused by the customer who must pay them.”29 Indeed, as the courts have held,

“nothing requires the Commission to ensure full or perfect cost causation,”30 and the

Commission “is not bound to reject any rate mechanism that tracks the cost causation

principle less than perfectly.”31

           Here, the data reported by Electric Distributors represent the most practical and

administratively feasible measure of incremental Large Load growth for purposes of

establishing a cost allocation approach that will assign costs to the zone/areas where the

incremental Large Loads will be located. While no cost allocation methodology can

achieve perfect precision, the Commission has repeatedly recognized that feasibility

considerations are relevant and that cost-causation principles need only be applied in a

reasonably accurate and practical manner.32 By relying on Electric Distributor’s reported


28
   Ill. Com. Comm’n, 576 F.3d at 477 (requiring “an articulable and plausible reason to believe that the
benefits are at least roughly commensurate with [the costs]”); Transmission Planning and Cost Allocation by
Transmission Owning and Operating Public Utilities, Order No. 1000, 136 FERC ¶ 61,051, at PP 622, 639
(2011) (requiring costs of regional transmission facilities to be allocated in a manner that is at least roughly
commensurate with estimated benefits), order on reh’g & clarification, Order No. 1000-A, 139 FERC
¶ 61,132, order on reh’g & clarification, Order No. 1000-B, 141 FERC ¶ 61,044 (2012), aff’d sub nom., S.C.
Pub. Serv. Auth. v. FERC, 762 F.3d 41 (D.C. Cir. 2014) (“South Carolina PSA”).
29

Transmission Owners, 373 F.3d at 1368 (quoting K N Energy, 968 F.2d at 1300)).
30

31

32

Comm’n of Wis. v. FERC, 545 F.3d 1058, 1066-67 (D.C. Cir. 2008); Carnegie Nat. Gas Co. v. FERC, 968
 Debbie-Anne Reese, Secretary
October 29, 2026

incremental Large Load growth at the zonal or area level, the proposal tracks the costs

associated with emerging Large Load demand to the most granular level that is reasonably

feasible and therefore satisfies the Commission’s cost-causation requirements.

           To be clear, the information required under this proposal will initially be reported

separately from the Large Load Registry that the Commission recently accepted because

the information required from the Electric Distributors serves a different purpose.

Specifically, the reporting requirement here is targeted to quantify incremental Large Load

growth between 2026 and the 2028/2029 Delivery Year for purposes of establishing the

Initial RBP Target. Nonetheless, to the extent appropriate, certain information submitted

through this process may ultimately be incorporated into the Large Load Registry.

                    2.      RBP costs will be allocated to the zone/areas associated with
                            incremental Large Loads.

           Based on information provided by Electric Distributors, PJM will allocate the

Initial RBP Target among Electric Distributor zone/areas in proportion to each zone/area’s

share of the total incremental Large Load growth. PJM will then reduce a zone/area’s

allocated share to the extent PJM receives the requisite evidence, as detailed in Tariff,

Attachment DD, section 18.2(c),33 of new capacity in the form of Qualifying RBP Offset

UCAP MW that is the subject of a bilateral agreement with a Large Load.34 In addition, to

the extent an Electric Distributor requests, with the required accompanying support

205, there is “no requirement in the Act itself that rates precisely match cost causation and responsibility”
and that instead “the Commission may rationally emphasize other, competing policies and approve measures
that do not best match cost responsibility and causation”).
33

Large Loads for at least five Delivery Years with a commercial operation date prior to the start of the
2032/2033 Delivery Year as further detailed in Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.2(c).

pursuant to Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.1(d), that the Initial RBP Target be

decremented to reflect the associated MW quantity of load participating in a qualifying

Peak Shaving Adjustment program, the Initial RBP Target may be further reduced.35 After

accounting for all Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW and any applicable Peak Shaving

Adjustment opt-out, PJM will determine each zone/area’s adjusted incremental Large Load

quantity.      That quantity, floored at zero, will serve as the basis for calculating the

zone/area’s pro rata share of the Final RBP Target MW. Ms. Danielle Croop, PJM’s senior

manager of market design, provides a detailed example that demonstrates how the RBP

obligations will be allocated to each Electric Distributor’s zone/area.36

           This approach is consistent with the Commission’s determination that “[a]llocating

RBP costs based on a snapshot of this shortfall over the term of the RBP commitment

period may provide greater certainty to the LSEs in the Electric Distributor zone/areas

ultimately bearing responsibility for those costs.”37            Accordingly, PJM proposes to

continue using a snapshot of incremental Large Load growth between the 2026 summer

peak and the forecasted summer peak for the 2028/2029 Delivery Year to establish each

zone/area’s share of the Final RBP Target MW. That allocation to the zone/area will

remain fixed throughout the 15-year RBP commitment period. Maintaining a fixed

allocation to the zone/area promotes certainty, provides transparent cost responsibility at

the outset of the commitment period, and avoids repeated reallocation of costs to different

zone/areas during the term of the RBP Resource commitment.

Aff.”).

                    3.       PJM will further allocate RBP Charges to relevant LSEs in the
                             zone/areas with incremental Large Loads.

           PJM is retaining the mechanism through which RBP Charges may be more

granularly allocated to LSEs within an Electric Distributor’s zone/area. As noted, above,

the September 29 Order held that “the ultimate cost allocation to the LSEs as determined

by the state and/or RERRA and as reported to the Electric Distributor . . . may be just and

reasonable[.]”38 Specifically, RBP Charges may be allocated based on “the state and/or

RERRA-determined allocation of cleared RBP UCAP MW to LSEs within each Electric

Distributor’s zone/area, as reported by each Electric Distributor to [PJM].”39 Likewise,

PJM is maintaining the term, “RBP Obligation” or “RBO” to provide flexibility for states

and/or RERRAs to further determine which retail customers should be allocated RBP

Charges.40

           The RBO framework provides states and RERRAs, through the relevant Electric
